subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 5 periods = 225 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 45min

periods.stage_label: Observe and question: what health really is
periods.activity_description: Students examine a case study of a student with social isolation and excessive screen time who develops physical and mental symptoms, then compare that profile against the WHO definition and the Ayurvedic view of health to surface the gap between absence-of-disease thinking and holistic health.

roles.role_description: Presents the case study and invites students to identify which dimensions of health are affected, then introduces the WHO and Ayurvedic definitions.
Reads the case study, notes which symptoms are physical, mental, or social, and records which definition best accounts for the full picture.
Compares individual notes in small groups and agrees on a working definition of health in their own words.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the case study of the student with screen-time habits and social isolation; students read and mark physical, mental, and social effects they notice.
Teacher introduces the WHO definition and the Ayurvedic perspective on balance of body, mind, and surroundings; students compare both definitions against the case study symptoms.
Small groups formulate a single agreed statement capturing what health means beyond absence of disease, drawing on both definitions and the case study evidence.
Groups share their statements; teacher facilitates a brief whole-class convergence on the three dimensions of health that will anchor the rest of the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit launches the chapter by immediately challenging the common student assumption that being healthy simply means not being ill — the case study makes that gap visible before any definition is given. Watch for students who conflate the mental and social dimensions, treating them as the same thing; the case study deliberately separates social isolation from anxiety to give you a concrete example to probe. A useful checkpoint before moving on is whether groups can name all three dimensions and locate at least one case-study detail in each.
materials: Printed or projected case study text from Activity 3.1
Whiteboard or chart paper for group statements

periods.stage_label: Classify and connect: lifestyle, environment, and staying healthy
periods.activity_description: Students sort a set of habit cards into helpful and harmful columns, justify their classification using criteria from the chapter, then connect each harmful habit to a specific dimension of health it threatens, producing a completed two-column table with justifications.

roles.role_description: Distributes habit cards and the classification table, then facilitates a whole-class debrief drawing out the link between environment (AQI, clean surroundings) and personal habits.
Sorts cards into helpful and harmful columns, records a justification for each placement, and identifies which health dimension each harmful habit affects.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly connects this unit to the previous one — the three dimensions of health just established now need to be linked to everyday practices — and distributes the habit cards and table.
Groups sort all cards, record justifications in the table, and flag any card they disagree about for class discussion.
Whole-class debrief: teacher draws out the AQI connection and asks how a clean environment fits alongside personal habits as a condition for health.
Students individually add one environmental habit (e.g. reducing vehicle use, maintaining clean surroundings) to their table, connecting it to the AQI concept from the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the three dimensions introduced in the previous unit — students now need to match lifestyle choices to those dimensions, not just name them. A common error is classifying processed or sugary food as merely a personal preference rather than a health-affecting habit; prompt groups to trace the pathway from that habit to a specific health outcome described in the chapter. If groups disagree on a card, treat it as a discussion prompt rather than correcting it immediately.
materials: Habit cards (one set per group, prepared from section 3.2.1 content — e.g. balanced diet, screen time, outdoor play, tobacco, yoga, adequate sleep)

periods.stage_label: Explain mechanisms: how diseases arise and spread
periods.activity_description: Students receive a partially completed transmission table for common communicable diseases and use the chapter's content to fill in causal agent, transmission route, site of infection, and one preventive measure, then identify patterns across transmission modes to construct a rule about how route of spread shapes prevention.

roles.role_description: Introduces pathogens and the communicable/non-communicable distinction, then poses the driving question: does the way a disease spreads determine how we prevent it?
Completes the transmission table and extracts a pattern linking transmission route to the most effective preventive measure for diseases in that group.
Writes a one-sentence rule stating the relationship between transmission route and prevention strategy, based on the group's completed table.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces pathogens, the two major disease types, and the five transmission routes from the chapter; students note these as a brief reference framework.

Groups work through the partially completed transmission table — airborne, waterborne/foodborne, and vector-borne diseases — filling in agent, route, infection site, and prevention for each disease listed.
Groups compare completed tables and identify which prevention strategies appear repeatedly for diseases sharing a route, articulating a pattern.
Each student writes an individual one-sentence rule connecting transmission route to prevention strategy; teacher collects or reads two or three aloud to check for causal reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit extends the classification work of the previous unit into causal mechanism — students must now explain why a disease spreads a particular way, not just name the route. A frequent misconception is that all diseases caused by insects are treated the same way as airborne diseases; the table's grouping by route is designed to make that error visible. Collecting individual sentences at the close gives you a quick diagnostic of which students can move from pattern to rule.
materials: Partially completed transmission table (adapted from Table 3.1, Activity 3.4)
Chapter summary or textbook for reference
homework: Select one NCD from section 3.4.2 (e.g. diabetes, asthma, or a deficiency disease) and write two sentences explaining which lifestyle or environmental factor causes it and which specific change could reduce the risk — do not list; explain the causal link.

periods.stage_label: Explain mechanisms: how diseases arise and spread
periods.activity_title: NCDs, Immunity, and the Science of Vaccines
periods.activity_description: Students examine the causal chain for non-communicable diseases, then follow Edward Jenner's scientific reasoning — observation, hypothesis, experiment, conclusion — to explain how vaccination produces acquired immunity, distinguishing vaccines from antibiotics and identifying what each can and cannot treat.

roles.role_description: Explains NCD causes, introduces immunity and the immune system, then walks students through Jenner's investigation using the Think-like-a-scientist framework from the chapter.
Records the stages of Jenner's reasoning and produces a comparison entry distinguishing vaccines from antibiotics by mechanism and target pathogen type.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects back to the transmission table from the previous unit, noting that NCDs have no pathogen chain, then explains the lifestyle and environmental causes of diabetes, cancer, and deficiency diseases.

Teacher presents Jenner's observation about cowpox and milkmaids, his hypothesis, his inoculation experiment, and the eventual eradication of smallpox, with students recording each stage of the reasoning.

Teacher introduces antibiotics and antibiotic resistance, explaining why antibiotics target bacterial cell structures and are ineffective against viruses or protozoa; students note target pathogen types.

Students individually complete a two-row comparison: vaccine (mechanism — trains immune system; target — bacteria or viruses preventively) versus antibiotic (mechanism — kills bacteria; target — bacteria only; ineffective against viruses).

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the disease-mechanism stage by pairing the communicable-disease causal chain from the previous unit with the biological response to it — immunity and treatment. The most persistent misconception here is that antibiotics cure viral illnesses like the common cold or flu; Jenner's example and the vaccine-versus-antibiotic comparison are both designed to surface and correct this directly. If time allows, ask students to explain why completing an antibiotic course matters, using the antibiotic resistance explanation from the chapter.
materials: Whiteboard or projected notes for Jenner's reasoning stages

periods.stage_label: Apply and evaluate: distinguishing holistic health from absence of disease through prevention and treatment reasoning
periods.activity_title: The Bhadrak Decision: Prevention vs Cure
periods.activity_description: Students analyse the Bhadrak sanitation case study to evaluate why a community-level sanitation intervention reduced communicable disease incidence, then apply that reasoning to a new scenario — a neighbourhood with rising NCD rates — to recommend a prevention and management strategy grounded in holistic health principles.

roles.role_description: Presents the Bhadrak case study and the new NCD-scenario prompt, then facilitates a whole-class discussion connecting both to the dissolution test's core question: what distinguishes holistic health from mere absence of disease?

Analyses the Bhadrak case study, traces how sanitation addressed the transmission route, then applies the same logical structure to the NCD scenario to produce a written prevention-and-management recommendation.

Writes a final response to the prompt: explain, using specific evidence from both scenarios, how lifestyle choices, environmental hygiene, immunity, and treatment together constitute holistic health rather than simply the absence of disease.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the Bhadrak case study and asks groups to identify which transmission route the sanitation campaign addressed and why that made it effective for communicable diseases.

Groups analyse Bhadrak, then receive the NCD-scenario prompt and work out which lifestyle and environmental factors are driving NCD rates and what combination of prevention, immunity support, and management would address them.
Groups share recommendations; teacher facilitates cross-group comparison highlighting that communicable and non-communicable disease prevention use different levers but both serve holistic health.

Students individually write their final response connecting the full arc — holistic health definition, lifestyle and environment, communicable and NCD causation, immunity, and treatment — to argue why prevention plus management is stronger than cure alone.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit asks students to synthesise every prior unit: the three dimensions of health, lifestyle and environment, disease causation and spread, and immunity and treatment are all brought to bear on two concrete scenarios. Watch for responses that correctly handle the communicable scenario but revert to listing habits for the NCD scenario without explaining causal links — the individual writing prompt is designed to push beyond listing toward reasoned argument. The Bhadrak example was chosen deliberately because it shows community-level action, connecting the social dimension of health students identified in the first unit.
materials: NCD-scenario prompt card (prepared by teacher, e.g.: 'A neighbourhood survey finds rising rates of diabetes and asthma. What combination of prevention, environmental change, immunity support, and management would you recommend and why?')

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and question: what health really is
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify the physical, mental, and social dimensions of health and explain, using case-study evidence, why the absence of disease is an insufficient definition of health.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: A student spends most of the day alone, avoids outdoor play, and reports headaches and difficulty concentrating at school, but has no diagnosed illness. According to the WHO definition of health, which statement best describes this student's condition?

options.label: A
options.text: The student is healthy because no disease has been diagnosed.

options.label: B
options.text: The student is not fully healthy because mental and social well-being are compromised even without a diagnosed disease.

options.label: C
options.text: The student is unhealthy only if a doctor confirms a physical disorder.

options.label: D
options.text: The student's health status cannot be judged without knowing their diet and exercise routine.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Selects this option: holds the common misconception that health means only the absence of diagnosed disease, ignoring the mental and social dimensions the WHO definition requires.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Selects this option: conflates health assessment with medical diagnosis, not recognising that the WHO definition extends beyond what doctors certify.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selects this option: confuses the lifestyle factors that sustain health with the definition of health itself, redirecting to habits rather than applying the three-dimensional definition.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find text-based scenarios difficult can be offered a verbal description of the case by the teacher before reading; the question stem can also be paired with the case-study image from Activity 3.1 to support visual learners.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and question: what health really is
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify the physical, mental, and social dimensions of health and explain, using case-study evidence, why the absence of disease is an insufficient definition of health.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: The Ayurvedic view of health, as described in the chapter, emphasises balance of body, mind, and surroundings supported by practices such as dinacharya and yoga. Which of the following best explains why this view goes beyond the idea that health means not falling sick?

options.label: A
options.text: It defines health as the result of following a fixed daily routine prescribed for everyone.

options.label: B
options.text: It focuses only on physical fitness through yoga and ignores mental and social factors.

options.label: C
options.text: It replaces modern medicine with traditional practices that prevent all diseases.

options.label: D
options.text: It treats health as an active, balanced state involving mental and environmental well-being, not just the absence of illness.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Selects this option: misreads the Ayurvedic perspective as a claim of disease eradication rather than a framework for holistic balance, confusing traditional medicine's scope with its philosophy.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Selects this option: reduces the Ayurvedic view to physical practice only, ignoring the explicit inclusion of mind and surroundings described in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Selects this option: conflates the specific practices of dinacharya and ritucharya with a rigid universal prescription, missing the underlying principle of balance across all three dimensions.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are less familiar with Ayurvedic terminology can be supported by a brief teacher gloss on dinacharya before the assessment; the question can also be answered by students who draw on the general principle rather than the specific term.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and connect: lifestyle, environment, and staying healthy
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can classify lifestyle and environmental factors as health-promoting or health-threatening and justify each classification by tracing its effect on a specific dimension of health.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: A city's Air Quality Index (AQI) rises sharply due to vehicle and factory pollution. A student argues that this only affects people who already have asthma and does not affect healthy people. Using the chapter's explanation of how environment contributes to health, which response best challenges this argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Environmental factors only affect the social dimension of health, not the physical dimension.

options.label: B
options.text: Poor air quality can cause respiratory problems even in people without prior illness, because a clean environment is a condition for health, not just for treatment.

options.label: C
options.text: The AQI measures pollution levels but has no direct link to human illness.

options.label: D
options.text: The AQI only matters if a person has a respiratory disease, so the student's argument is correct.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Selects this option: holds the misconception that environmental factors only affect those already ill, failing to connect AQI to health as a preventive condition for everyone.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Selects this option: confuses the AQI as a monitoring tool with a claim that it is merely a measurement, not recognising the chapter's explicit link between AQI values and asthma and respiratory problems.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Selects this option: incorrectly assigns environmental factors exclusively to the social dimension, splitting the physical and environmental causes of health in a way the chapter does not support.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the AQI concept abstract can be asked to substitute a concrete image from Activity 3.3 — the polluted playground — as the scenario context; the reasoning required is identical.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and connect: lifestyle, environment, and staying healthy
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can classify lifestyle and environmental factors as health-promoting or health-threatening and justify each classification by tracing its effect on a specific dimension of health.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: Two students discuss their daily routines. Student X eats processed food, sleeps fewer hours than recommended, and spends most free time on screens. Student Y eats a balanced diet with fruits and vegetables, plays outdoors, and gets adequate sleep. Which explanation correctly connects their different routines to likely health outcomes?

options.label: A
options.text: Screen time is not a health factor because it does not involve ingesting any substance.

options.label: B
options.text: Student X's routine increases the risk of NCDs because processed food, inadequate sleep, and low physical activity are lifestyle factors the chapter links to disease.

options.label: C
options.text: Student X's routine is only a concern if there is a family history of disease, since genetics determines outcomes more than lifestyle.

options.label: D
options.text: Student Y's routine prevents all communicable diseases because a balanced diet eliminates pathogens.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Selects this option: over-weights genetics relative to lifestyle, contradicting the chapter's explicit claim that NCDs arise from lifestyle, diet, and environmental factors.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selects this option: overgeneralises the protective effect of a healthy diet, incorrectly claiming it prevents communicable diseases by eliminating pathogens rather than supporting overall health.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Selects this option: uses a narrow definition of health harm (ingestion only), missing the chapter's connection between excessive screen time, social isolation, and physical and mental health impacts.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with comparing two characters can be asked to analyse only Student X's routine first and then state one contrast with Student Y; the cognitive operation required is the same.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and connect: lifestyle, environment, and staying healthy
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can classify lifestyle and environmental factors as health-promoting or health-threatening and justify each classification by tracing its effect on a specific dimension of health.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that even a clean physical environment cannot compensate for poor emotional or social well-being. Describe one specific situation that illustrates this claim and identify the dimension of health it demonstrates.
expected_elements: A specific situation in which physical surroundings are clean but a person's emotional or social well-being is poor (e.g. social isolation despite living in a clean home, peer exclusion in a clean school environment).
Identification of the mental or social dimension of health as the one being compromised in that situation.
A brief explanation of why the clean environment alone is insufficient to produce good health in that situation.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find it difficult to generate their own scenario can be offered the case study from Activity 3.1 as a starting point and asked to explain why that student's health remains poor despite the family's otherwise clean home environment.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Disease | Causal Agent | Transmission Route | Preventive Measure
Malaria | Protozoa | Vector (mosquito) | Eliminate stagnant water; use mosquito nets
Typhoid | Bacteria | Contaminated food or water | Boil water; maintain food hygiene
Influenza | Virus | Airborne (coughs, sneezes) | Cover mouth; wear masks
Hepatitis A | Virus | Contaminated food or water | Hand hygiene; safe food preparation
assessment_items.question_text: A new disease X is identified. Its causal agent is a bacterium that spreads when an infected person coughs near others. Refer to the table provided. Based on patterns in the table, which preventive measure is most appropriate for disease X, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Avoid handshaking, because bacteria spread by direct contact between people.

options.label: B
options.text: Boil all drinking water, because the causal agent is a bacterium and bacteria spread through water.

options.label: C
options.text: Cover the mouth when coughing and wear masks, because the airborne transmission route requires blocking expelled droplets, as seen for other airborne diseases in the table.

options.label: D
options.text: Eliminate stagnant water, because bacteria breed in water.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Selects this option: incorrectly associates bacteria with water as a transmission medium in all cases, confusing typhoid's waterborne route with the airborne route of disease X.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Selects this option: over-applies the link between bacteria and water, conflating the causal agent type with the transmission route — the table shows typhoid uses contaminated water, but disease X spreads by coughing, not water.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Selects this option: confuses airborne transmission with direct contact, applying the prevention strategy for direct-contact diseases to a disease whose transmission route is airborne.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to extract the pattern from the full table can be directed to compare only influenza and disease X first, isolating the matching transmission route before selecting a prevention strategy.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain mechanisms: how diseases arise and spread
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can explain how communicable diseases spread and are prevented by tracing transmission routes, and can explain how the body resists disease through immunity and vaccines, distinguishing these from antibiotics and their limitations.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: A doctor diagnoses a patient with a viral infection and prescribes rest and fluids, but does not prescribe antibiotics. A family member insists the patient should take antibiotics to recover faster. Which explanation best justifies the doctor's decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Antibiotics are too expensive for routine use and should be reserved for serious diseases only.

options.label: B
options.text: Antibiotics kill bacteria by targeting structures absent in human cells but are ineffective against viruses, so prescribing them for a viral infection would not aid recovery and risks contributing to antibiotic resistance.

options.label: C
options.text: Antibiotics only work after a vaccine has been given, so they cannot be used as a first treatment.

options.label: D
options.text: Antibiotics weaken the immune system, so doctors avoid them whenever immunity can fight the disease.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Selects this option: replaces the biological explanation with a cost-based rationale, indicating the student has not engaged with the chapter's explanation of how antibiotics work and their specific target.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selects this option: holds a misconception that antibiotics suppress rather than supplement the immune system, conflating the chapter's antibiotic resistance discussion with a claim about immune weakening.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Selects this option: confuses the sequence of vaccination and antibiotic use, incorrectly treating them as sequential steps rather than independent biological mechanisms with different targets.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the mechanism can be asked to recall what Alexander Fleming's discovery targeted and then apply that to the scenario before choosing an option.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can explain how communicable diseases spread and are prevented by tracing transmission routes, and can explain how the body resists disease through immunity and vaccines, distinguishing these from antibiotics and their limitations.

assessment_items.question_text: Edward Jenner observed that milkmaids who had cowpox did not contract smallpox. Describe the two-step reasoning Jenner used to move from this observation to a testable experiment, and state what the result of that experiment demonstrated about immunity.
expected_elements: Statement of Jenner's hypothesis: exposure to cowpox produces protection against smallpox.
Description of the experimental step: inoculating a person with cowpox material and then exposing them to smallpox to test whether protection resulted.
Statement of what the result demonstrated: that acquired immunity can be produced by controlled exposure to a weakened or related pathogen, forming the basis of vaccination.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find it difficult to articulate the two-step reasoning in prose can be asked to present their answer as two labelled points — Hypothesis and Experiment — before writing a concluding sentence on the result.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can distinguish holistic health from mere absence of disease by explaining how communicable and non-communicable diseases arise, spread, and can be prevented through lifestyle choices, environmental hygiene, immunity, and appropriate treatment, and can evaluate a prevention-and-management strategy against that framework.

assessment_items.question_text: In Bhadrak district, a community sanitation campaign that improved toilet use and reduced open defecation led to fewer cases of diarrhoea and infections in children. A health worker argues this is a better long-term strategy than distributing antibiotics to treat each child when they fall sick. Which evaluation of the health worker's argument is best supported by the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: The argument is correct because improving sanitation addresses the transmission route of waterborne and contact diseases, reducing incidence at the source rather than treating each case after infection.

options.label: B
options.text: The argument is incorrect because antibiotics are always more reliable than sanitation for controlling bacterial infections.

options.label: C
options.text: The argument is irrelevant because children's immunity is naturally strong enough to overcome diarrhoea without either sanitation or antibiotics.

options.label: D
options.text: The argument is partially correct but only applies to NCDs, since communicable diseases always require antibiotic treatment.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Selects this option: inverts the chapter's prevention-over-cure principle, treating antibiotics as the primary strategy and ignoring the chapter's explicit illustration of sanitation reducing disease incidence.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selects this option: incorrectly restricts the principle of prevention to NCDs, conflating the NCD lifestyle-change discussion with the Bhadrak communicable-disease prevention example.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Selects this option: over-relies on natural immunity to dismiss both prevention and treatment, ignoring the chapter's evidence that sanitation campaigns demonstrably reduced childhood infections.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to evaluate the argument abstractly can be prompted to first identify which disease type diarrhoea is and which transmission route it uses, and then decide which strategy interrupts that route.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply and evaluate: distinguishing holistic health from absence of disease through prevention and treatment reasoning
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can distinguish holistic health from mere absence of disease by explaining how communicable and non-communicable diseases arise, spread, and can be prevented through lifestyle choices, environmental hygiene, immunity, and appropriate treatment, and can evaluate a prevention-and-management strategy against that framework.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: A government health programme declares victory over disease in a district because the number of patients hospitalised for communicable infections has dropped to zero. Critics argue the district is not yet fully healthy. Which argument best supports the critics' position, based on the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: The critics are correct because communicable diseases can never reach zero unless every resident has received every available vaccine.

options.label: B
options.text: The critics are correct because non-communicable diseases linked to lifestyle and environment, and poor mental and social well-being, can persist even when communicable disease incidence is zero.

options.label: C
options.text: The critics are wrong — zero hospitalisations for communicable disease means the district has achieved complete health.

options.label: D
options.text: The critics are wrong because once communicable diseases are eliminated, NCDs automatically decline due to improved immunity.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Selects this option: retains the misconception that health equals absence of disease — the very misconception the chapter opens by challenging — applying it at the population level.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Selects this option: conflates the critics' argument with a separate claim about vaccination coverage, missing the holistic-health argument and instead replacing it with a communicable-disease-control claim.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selects this option: incorrectly links communicable disease elimination to automatic NCD decline through immunity, confusing the immune system's role in fighting pathogens with the lifestyle and environmental causes of NCDs.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find population-level scenarios difficult can be asked to substitute a single person who has no communicable illness but has diabetes and social isolation, and then decide whether that person is fully healthy.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can distinguish holistic health from mere absence of disease by explaining how communicable and non-communicable diseases arise, spread, and can be prevented through lifestyle choices, environmental hygiene, immunity, and appropriate treatment, and can evaluate a prevention-and-management strategy against that framework.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: A neighbourhood survey shows that residents are free from communicable diseases but have high rates of diabetes and respiratory problems. Some residents are socially isolated and report low well-being. Using the chapter's framework, evaluate whether this neighbourhood is healthy, and propose a strategy that addresses all dimensions of the problem. Justify each element of your strategy by linking it to a specific cause described in the chapter.
look_for: Explicitly states that the neighbourhood is not fully healthy, using the WHO or Ayurvedic three-dimensional definition as justification — absence of communicable disease is not sufficient.
Identifies lifestyle and environmental factors (processed food, inactivity, pollution) as causes of the high NCD rates, linking each factor to the specific disease mentioned.
Addresses the social isolation dimension with a strategy connected to the social dimension of health, not just physical or environmental factors.
Proposes prevention strategies grounded in the chapter — lifestyle changes, environmental hygiene, community engagement — rather than only treatment.
Distinguishes where vaccination or antibiotic treatment would be relevant versus where lifestyle management and early diagnosis are the appropriate response for NCDs.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to structure a full evaluative response can be guided to write three labelled sections — Is this neighbourhood healthy? (with justification), What is causing the problems? (with causes), and What would help? (with strategy and link to cause) — before integrating them into prose.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply and evaluate: distinguishing holistic health from absence of disease through prevention and treatment reasoning
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can distinguish holistic health from mere absence of disease by explaining how communicable and non-communicable diseases arise, spread, and can be prevented through lifestyle choices, environmental hygiene, immunity, and appropriate treatment, and can evaluate a prevention-and-management strategy against that framework.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Situation | Disease Type | Transmission Route or Cause | Nature of Substance or Factor | Prevention or Management Strategy | Treatment Approach
Children in a village develop diarrhoea after the monsoon floods the water supply | | | | |
Factory workers in a city develop asthma after years of exposure to chemical fumes | | | | |
A teenager avoids outdoor activity, eats processed food daily, and is found to have early-stage diabetes | | | | |
A student develops chickenpox after contact with an infected classmate | | | | |
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each situation: (1) identify whether the disease is communicable or non-communicable and state the transmission route or cause; (2) identify the specific factor (pathogen, lifestyle factor, or environmental factor) responsible; (3) propose one prevention or management strategy; (4) state the appropriate treatment approach and explain why it fits this disease type.
assessment_items.scaffold: Use the chapter's classification of communicable and non-communicable diseases, the transmission routes described in Section 3.4.1, and the prevention and treatment principles from Section 3.5. For each row, complete all four columns before moving to the next situation.
format_of_output: Completed table with all four columns filled for each of the four situations.
A concluding sentence (below the table) stating, in your own words, what the four situations together show about why holistic health requires more than the absence of communicable disease.

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The Final Stage implied LO requires the student to distinguish holistic health from mere absence of disease by reasoning across communicable disease, NCD, lifestyle, environment, immunity, and treatment simultaneously — a classification-with-justification task across four contrasting scenarios is the most direct demonstration vehicle for that integrated operation.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can apply the chapter's full framework — disease type classification, transmission route or causal factor identification, prevention strategy selection, and treatment approach justification — across both communicable and non-communicable disease scenarios, integrating all four chapter mechanisms rather than handling them in isolation.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The four situations are designed to span all major disease categories in the chapter: waterborne communicable, environmentally caused NCD, lifestyle NCD, and airborne communicable. A student who completes all four columns correctly for all four situations has demonstrated breadth; the concluding sentence reveals whether they can abstract a principle from the pattern. Watch especially for the concluding sentence — it is the truest test of whether the student has internalised the holistic health argument.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses correctly classify all four disease types, trace each to a specific cause from the chapter rather than a generic statement, select prevention strategies that match the identified transmission route or causal factor, and write a concluding sentence that articulates the holistic health principle rather than restating a single row. Weak responses misclassify at least one NCD as communicable, propose treatment-only responses for the NCD rows without mentioning lifestyle change or prevention, and write a concluding sentence that lists facts rather than drawing a principle.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find all four rows demanding can be asked to complete only the diarrhoea row and the diabetes row — one communicable and one NCD — before attempting the others; the concluding sentence can be written on the basis of those two contrasting cases alone and still demonstrates the core cognitive operation.
